doc.title: Luis Conte interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 24, 2025

chapter: Finding the drums at Los Angeles City College
title: Discovering Mongo, Puente, Fania and Los Angeles drum circles
summary: Having never heard the exiled Cuban percussionists, Conte learned of Mongo Santamaria, Tito Puente and Fania records, found Griffith Park drum circles disorganized, and bought Colon, Puente and Palmieri albums.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: No man. Maybe it’s because I listened to so much American music as a kid. I just – oh, [scats] it’s timbao – it’s what we call timbao in Afro-Cuban, but just swing it. That’s all it is. You know. But at that time I had never heard of Chano Pozo, I had never heard of any of this. I didn’t know anything man. I really didn’t – of any of the – I started finding out who – I never heard of Mongo Santamaria, I had never heard of Tito Puente, I had never heard of Patato Valdes. These are guys that had left. I knew Papin, Tata Guines, you know etcetera etcetera when I was a boy. But the guys that were out here – so I’m just, I don't know, I’m floating, man. You know.
I bet you had some revelations along the way. I mean at that time there was some hit records by those fellas. Like “Watermelon Man” and some of the more accessible tunes.

Yeah, yeah. And I started hearing all this stuff from other friends that knew about this, “Oh right, you’ve got to listen – Mongo,” you know, so-and-so, that I had met. I met -- another guy that was going to LACC also, his name was John Montealegre was his last name. He was an African-American man but with the last name Montealegre and he lives in Pasadena, and he had a set of congas. So we hit it off, and I would go and hang out with him with a couple of friends, you know young guys you know just partying Friday night, Saturday night, over at his house it was just like listening to music and other guys who were like I found out about Fania, the label Fania that was the big of what they call salsa now of Cuban music. The label is Willie Colon and Eddie Palmieri. I went to a park out here, Griffith Park that was guys would get together and play drums. And I called them “thunder drummers” because I was used to hearing – when you play in Cuba in a percussion ensemble is playing. You know you play with a bunch of conga players and you have a comparsa or something in carnival. I mean everything is organized. All the parts are organized. Over here it’s like a drum circle. You know over here you’ve got guys that just go [scats]. So I kind of went like well this is not quite happening. But one day there was a – I heard some other stuff under some other tree. And there was this Cuban dude and this Puerto Rican cat and he had a – this is how I found out about Fania – he had a cassette and he was Willie Colon. And I went, “Dude, that’s Cuban music.” And he said, “Well yeah, this is from New York.” I says, “But yeah, who is this?” He said, “Well this is Willie Colon.” I says, “Well where do you get these records?” And there was one – at that time, this was the ‘70s – one record shop that carried this music. And it was downtown L.A. called Doran Music. So I went there, whatever little money I © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

had I bought a Willie Colon record, I bought a Puente album, and I bought an Eddie Palmieri “Azucar Pa Ti.” I still have them. And it’s just – it was all happening man. But it just, you know for me to go into, if you play a little funk I’ll just figure something out. And I’ve heard the tambourines and I’ve heard all that before. I’ll say one thing I would know – sometimes if you listen to some songs – I can’t think of them now – sometimes the conga pattern was turned around as a Cuban would play it. You know and it was like [scats] and I would go okay, well – that’s not even right.
It sounded more like you were doing like what a tom-tom – drummer might do on their tom-toms.
